title: Lock TTL Fence Token Mismatch

# Lock TTL Fence Token Mismatch

**Category:** Debugging  
**Difficulty:** Hard  

## Scenario

A cache rebuild job overwrote fresh product data with an older snapshot after its lock expired. The lock dashboard shows the original worker still writing after a newer worker acquired the same key. Search results briefly served stale prices and support caught it through screenshots. The next catalog import is larger, so this cannot be left to luck. Fix the lock and write path so stale owners cannot commit work.

## Background

The import path takes a short-lived lock, does expensive work, and writes output with a token that should prove ownership. Renewals happen during long imports, and lock expiry is expected when workers pause. Downstream caches trust the write record they receive. A worker with an old token must be rejected even if it still has the data it built.

## System Context

- Requests move through ownership, validation, state changes, audit, and external side effects.
- Tokens, scope, or decisions produced early in the flow are consumed by later steps.
- Operators rely on stable result payloads when reconstructing incidents.
- Retried or overlapping work is normal and must not corrupt unrelated records.

## Constraints

- Preserve public entry points and result dictionary keys.
- Reject stale or invalid work without blocking unrelated valid work.
- Keep audit events useful for successful and rejected transitions.
- Do not rely on real services, threads, or wall-clock time in tests.

## Your Task

- Fix the TTL and fence-token behavior around guarded writes.
- Keep the layered behavior clear enough to diagnose failures.
- Preserve Python 3.10+ compatibility.

# soul.md prebake · #44 Lock TTL Fence Token Mismatch

## What this problem really tests

**Discriminating problem-statement framing from concrete code gaps**: a scenario may invoke a rich industry concept (multiple protections, infrastructure-level guarantees) but the actual code base may only need a subset of that. Knowing how much of the framing to implement versus how much to leave as narrative is part of the work.

You're also tested on **version-bounded ownership verification** at the layer that processes writes — when a holder of an older version of an ownership claim tries to perform a state change, the system must refuse.

And on **composing multiple protection mechanisms**: production systems often pair a time-bounded protection with a version-bounded protection, each defending a different failure mode. Recognizing which protection a given test actually requires is part of scoping the fix.

## Good prompts to give your AI

- "List every concept the problem statement references. For each, find whether the existing code already has plumbing for it, or whether it's narrative without code."
- "Of the gaps you find, which ones do the failing tests actually exercise? Fix those; treat the rest as framing."
- "Look at the sibling problem family if there is one. Are the code structures identical? What does that tell you about the bug class?"
- "What separates two distinct rejection categories that share the same status string in a naive implementation? Could the audit trail tell them apart?"
- "When the problem invokes 'expiry' or 'renewal', do those concepts have any state representation in the model? If not, the code path isn't asking you to implement them."

## Reflexes to fight

- **Extending the data model with fields the existing serialized shape doesn't expose** — the shape is contract; new fields can break tests that pin the serialized representation
- **Wiring real-time timers or background threads** — the test fixture is deliberately in-memory and time-controlled; production infrastructure shouldn't leak into unit-test scope
- **Trying to implement every concept the problem statement mentions** — match the failing tests, not the prose surface area
- **Modifying public entry-point signatures or result dictionary keys** — those are observable contract for callers
- **Conflating distinct rejection categories under a single audit signal** — operators triaging incidents need to distinguish reasons

## Design patterns / concepts this problem maps to

- **Version-bounded ownership** — monotonic version stamps as ownership proofs (Kleppmann's fencing token writeup is the canonical reference)
- **Time-bounded ownership** — TTL-based ownership with renewal protocols (etcd leases, Redlock TTL, Zookeeper ephemeral nodes)
- **Two-protection pairing** — production systems often combine version-bound and time-bound; each defends a separate failure mode
- **Storage-layer vs service-layer verification** — the same check can live at either layer; consistent enforcement at one layer is what matters
- **Narrative-vs-code-gap discrimination** — problem statements set context; tests set scope; match scope, acknowledge context

## When to ask tips-agent for help

| Situation | What to ask |
|---|---|
| Trying to decide whether to implement TTL infrastructure | "Which failing tests reference expiry or clock advancement? If none, TTL is framing, not requirement." |
| Tempted to add fields to the data model | "What's the model's serialized output? Is the new field part of it? If yes, you may be modifying a contract." |
| Looking at a sibling problem (lease/lock pair) | "If the code structures are identical, the bug class is likely the same. Start there." |
| Audit log can't distinguish two failure modes | "Are operators going to need to know which mode caused the rejection? If yes, separate signals." |
| About to wire real-time infrastructure | "Look at the clock used in tests. Production timing primitives don't belong in unit-scope solutions." |

## Reading the failing tests as the source of truth

The problem framing tells you what concept space you're in. The tests tell you which concepts must work today. Stay strictly within "what tests need" and let the rest of the framing inform code comments, not code paths.

## Self-check before submitting

- Did your fix make every failing test pass without expanding the data model?
- Did your fix avoid wiring infrastructure (timing, threading, external services) that the test fixture doesn't use?
- Did your fix preserve every public signature and serialized shape?
- Did your fix produce distinct rejection signals for distinct failure reasons?
- Did you scope the fix to what tests demand, leaving richer framing in comments rather than code?
- For teaching variant: did you anchor your design with multiple industry references that show both protection mechanisms?
